title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 5: Legal Problems in International Trade Spawned by the AFTA
keywords: Legal Problems in International Trade Spawned by the AFTA
Framework Agreement on Enhancing ASEAN Economic Cooperation
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- the paper CJP presented before the 16th World Law Conference of the World Jurist Association on October 27, 1993, arguing that the Asean Free Trade Area has spawned new legal problems that AFTA's own documents do not solve, and that no free trade arrangement can succeed without an accompanying legal system.

A survey of the post-Cold War shift from military dominance to economic pre-eminence, and of the trade blocs it produced -- the European Community's Single European Market, NAFTA, and Asean's answer in AFTA.

A technical exposition of the CEPT scheme adopted at the 4th Asean Summit: the 15-year timetable from January 1, 1993, the fast track and normal track tariff reductions, the temporary and permanent exclusion lists, the 40 percent origin rule, and the removal of quantitative restrictions and non-tariff barriers.

Seven legal problems CJP identifies in AFTA -- absent dispute settlement, no implementing authority, double taxation, dumping through free ports, non-tariff barriers, CEPT's limited scope, and the unresolved need for ratification -- with the conclusion that legal harmonization must be built concurrently with the trade bloc.
sub_topics: The post-Soviet setting: with the balance of terror dismantled and long-term international peace not seriously doubted, 'Pax Americana' has arrived and leaders now rivet their attention on economic pre-eminence.

The competition for trade: newly industrializing Pacific Rim states as role models, and the escalation of come-ons from flags-of-convenience, secret bank accounts and tax havens to fiscal incentives, autonomous foreign trade zones and free ports.

The emergence of trade blocs as the successor to single-country effort, quoted through Foreign Affairs Secretary Roberto R. Romulo's definition of a bloc as countries establishing market conditions for themselves that differ from those applied to non-members.

The European Community as the most advanced bloc: the 'Europhoria' of the Single European Market of December 1992 covering 380 million customers, set back by the tumultuous ratification of the Maastricht Treaty, the monetary crisis, German unification, recession and Balkan strife.

NAFTA as the North American response: signed December 17, 1992, effective January 1, 1994, more than US$6 trillion in output and 360 million people, eliminating tariffs within 10 to 15 years and protecting intellectual property.

Asean's answer: the three documents adopted at the 4th Asean Summit in Singapore on January 27-28, 1992 -- the Singapore Declaration, the Framework Agreement and the CEPT Agreement -- responding to 'large and powerful economic groupings among the developed countries.'

The nine agreed features of AFTA: establishment within 15 years by 2008; CEPT as the main mechanism; progressive tariff reduction for pre-identified manufactures with agriculture excluded; the fast track of fifteen products to 0-5 percent within 7-10 years and the normal track over 10-15 years; temporary and permanent exclusion lists; the 40 percent origin requirement; elimination of quantitative restrictions; removal of other non-tariff barriers within five years; and cooperation on standards, testing, investment, macroeconomic consultation and venture capital.

The adverse effects of blocs, illustrated by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's claim that swift implementation will convince investors Asean is a serious player: trade diversion (Philippine exports priced out of the US against tariff-protected Mexican goods under NAFTA) and investment diversion toward member-countries.

Legal problem one -- settlement of disputes: a ministerial council but no judicial or quasi-judicial mechanism, no formal procedure, no statement of binding authority, an Article 12 escape for national security, morals, health and artistic property, and no mechanism at all for disputes between private producers of CEPT products.

Legal problem two -- implementing authority: Asean has created no institutional mechanism with sufficient resources and power, and Sree Kumar's ten-item list of tasks it would have to take up, from drawing a charter to designing a non-tariff-barrier removal strategy.

Legal problem three -- double taxation: Lawan Thanadsillapakul's distinction between juridical double taxation (the same income of the same person taxed by more than one state) and economic double taxation (two persons taxed on the same income), to be cured by bilateral or multilateral tax treaties.

Legal problems four and five -- dumping through free ports such as Singapore's and Subic's, to be met by policing goods and listing CEPT industries; and non-tariff barriers, which should be phased out over the same period as the tariffs rather than in five years.

Legal problem six -- CEPT's limited scope: unlike the EC and NAFTA, which open borders to goods, services, capital and people, CEPT merely reduces tariffs on pre-identified manufactures, excludes agriculture, and lets members exclude their own protected products at absolute discretion.

Legal problem seven -- ratification: the 1987 Constitution requires Senate concurrence for treaties and international agreements, yet Joseph Sedfrey S. Santiago's no-ratification view is being followed in practice, and CJP urges a second look given NAFTA's signatories' care over their own constitutional requirements.

The conclusion: trade liberalization is the wave of the future, but developing governments cannot simply open their borders; regional blocs are an intermediate protective step that will fail without a complementary review, updating and harmonization of laws, regulations and adjudicatory systems.

stances.claim: AFTA's dispute-settlement arrangement is inadequate: the CEPT Agreement provides only amicable settlement and referral to a ministerial council, with no judicial or quasi-judicial mechanism, no statement of binding authority, an Article 12 escape clause, and no mechanism at all for disputes between private producers.
stances.rhetorical_move: text-against-text: quoting the agreements' own dispute clauses to show what they omit, then contrasting political with judicial or arbitral settlement

stances.claim: CEPT's scope is too limited to succeed: it reduces tariffs only on pre-identified manufactures, excludes agriculture, provides nothing for services, capital and people, and permits members to exclude their own protected products at absolute discretion -- protectionist clauses that may diminish AFTA's chances.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparison-to-benchmark: measuring CEPT against the EC's and NAFTA's opening of goods, services, capital and people

stances.claim: The AFTA documents arguably require Senate concurrence, notwithstanding the no-ratification view already being followed by the Philippine government, because the Constitution's express language covers not only treaties but 'international agreements' and the documents create both rights and obligations beyond tariff-lowering.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-text-plus-comparative-practice, offered as 'an arguable case' and a call to take a second look rather than a flat conclusion

stances.claim: Developing-country governments cannot simply open their borders to multinationals; regional blocs are a legitimate intermediate step to level the playing field, but the step fails without concurrent review, updating and harmonization of laws, regulations and adjudicatory systems.
stances.rhetorical_move: means-not-end framing: AFTA recast as preparation for global competition, with legal harmonization as the condition of its success

notable_anecdotes: The catalogue of come-ons: he traces the escalation of state inducements from 'the simple and familiar flags-of-convenience, secret bank accounts and tax havens' of Liberia, the Netherlands Antilles, the Cayman Islands, Liechtenstein and the British Virgin Islands to trade zones and free ports.

'Europhoria': he uses the coinage for the EC's mood on establishing the Single European Market in December 1992, then sets against it the tumultuous Maastricht ratification, the monetary crisis, German unification, recession and Balkan strife.
The Mexican example of trade diversion: Philippine exports to the US made costlier to American customers than similar Mexican products enjoying tariff protection under NAFTA.
The free-port loophole: non-member countries unloading dumped or bulk goods at Singapore or Subic and recycling or repackaging them into the rest of Asean.

The editor's note records that the paper was presented when regional trading blocs were 'not generally understood by the legal community' and was reprinted in the Lawyers Review, Foreign Affairs Journal, Philippine Business and leading law school journals.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reproduces the paper Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban presented before the 16th World Law Conference of the World Jurist Association at the Philippine International Convention Center on October 27, 1993. He begins from the post-Cold War setting -- the Soviet Union dissolved, the balance of terror dismantled, 'Pax Americana' arrived -- in which leaders now rivet their attention on economic pre-eminence and states compete for trade through tax havens, incentives, foreign trade zones and free ports. That competition, he says, has outgrown single-country effort and produced trade blocs, which he defines through Foreign Affairs Secretary Roberto R. Romulo and illustrates through the European Community's 'Europhoria' over the Single European Market of December 1992 (set back by the tumultuous Maastricht ratification, the monetary crisis, German unification, recession and Balkan strife) and NAFTA, signed December 17, 1992 and effective January 1, 1994. Asean's answer was AFTA, built on the three documents adopted at the 4th Asean Summit of January 27-28, 1992, whose nine features he sets out in detail: establishment within fifteen years by 2008, the CEPT scheme as the main mechanism, a fast track of fifteen products to 0-5 percent within seven to ten years and a normal track over ten to fifteen, temporary and permanent exclusion lists, a 40 percent origin rule, elimination of quantitative restrictions, and removal of other non-tariff barriers within five years. He then names the resulting harms -- trade diversion and investment diversion -- and devotes the body of the paper to seven legal problems: the absence of any judicial or quasi-judicial dispute-settlement mechanism (and none at all for private producers), the absence of an institutional implementing authority, double taxation in its juridical and economic forms, dumping through free ports such as Singapore's and Subic's, non-tariff barriers phased out faster than the tariffs, CEPT's narrow scope compared with the EC's and NAFTA's opening of goods, services, capital and people, and the unresolved question whether the three documents require Senate concurrence under the 1987 Constitution, which he argues deserves a second look despite the government's contrary practice. He concludes that trade liberalization is the wave of the future but that developing governments cannot open their borders unprotected; regional blocs are only an intermediate step, and AFTA will fail unless the laws, regulations and adjudicatory systems of the member-countries are reviewed, updated and harmonized concurrently with the bloc itself.
